summary:
Honduran law does not criminalise gender identity, and same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1899 with the age of consent set at 15 years for both same-sex and heterosexual conduct.

The Penal Code, amended by Decree No. 23-2013 and in force since March 2017, treats hatred or contempt based on sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating circumstance in criminal responsibility under Article 27. Article 321 punishes anyone who arbitrarily blocks, restricts or denies individual or collective rights, or refuses a professional service, on those grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages. Article 321-A punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred, contempt, persecution, violence or attacks on those grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of L.50,000 to L.300,000. LGBTQ rights groups met with Congress before the new code took effect to ensure these provisions survived; they did.

The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs permits police to arrest anyone who 'goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals'. LGBTQ rights organisations have documented numerous instances of police using this provision as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space.

Violence against transgender people is documented and impunity is systemic. Human Rights Watch's May 2009 report 'Not Worth a Penny' documented police rape, assault and extortion of transgender people in Honduras. The LAWG Education Fund report 'Left in the Dark' finds that Honduras has among the world's highest rates of violence against women and LGBTI persons, that transgender women especially face major obstacles to justice, and that impunity is driven by under-reporting, lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources, and intentional case mishandling. The US State Department's 2021 Human Rights Report lists violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture, and lack of accountability for gender-based violence among significant human-rights issues. Documented killings include transgender activist Cynthia Nicole shot dead on 2 January 2022 and trans activist Thalia Rodriguez murdered on 10 January 2022 in Tegucigalpa; sixty-nine transgender people were among 174 violent LGBTQ deaths recorded from 2009 to 2014, and 264 LGBTQ people were murdered between 2009 and 2017, with those totals reported as raw counts by year range rather than per-capita rates. In June 2013 a trans woman was granted asylum in Spain after a police officer attempted to assassinate her.

Vicky Hernandez v Honduras, heard at the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case; Human Rights Watch finds that Central American states exclude transgender women from femicide legal frameworks, with Guatemalan officials describing them as 'not biological women'.

Transgender women are held in the men's prison system. Corresponsales Clave, drawing on the torture-prevention centre CPTRT, reports that at Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the 'La Isla' module beside the mentally-ill unit, that trans women are forced to cut their hair and barred from presenting as women, and that conjugal visits are denied. At Penitenciaria de Marcala authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair; only after CPTRT intervention was she isolated from the men and her belongings returned. Placement operates by birth sex with de facto LGBTI grouping and ad-hoc protective isolation, and no placement-by-gender-identity policy exists. Human Rights Watch (7 October 2020) independently confirms that Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, where physical and sexual abuse can follow: a Honduran judge told HRW of a trans woman raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards, and said she had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate. The judge's assessment was that there is no way to protect trans women in men's prisons.

Same-sex unions are not legally recognised. Decree 36 of 4 May 2005 amended Constitution Articles 112 and 116 to provide that only a man and a woman who have that status naturally may contract marriage, to prohibit marriage and de facto union between persons of the same sex, to refuse recognition of same-sex marriages or unions performed legally in other countries, and to bar same-sex couples from adopting. Same-sex couples and same-sex-headed households are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. A name change for LGBTI persons is approved, though the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association described it as an 'aberration in God's eyes'; no procedure details are given.

The Government offers medical care to all citizens and has worked increasingly with non-governmental organisations on HIV/AIDS awareness, but the socially conservative influence of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestants has made comprehensive public programmes difficult to implement. Female prostitutes and men who have sex with men are identified as the highest-risk groups. No youth-specific care or medication provisions appear.

Political hostility is visible. The two major parties have mostly ignored LGBTQ rights; only a handful of dissident members of the Democratic Unification Party expressed interest in working with the LGBT community; and three candidates who backed same-sex marriage before the November 2017 elections all failed to win National Congress seats. President Juan Orlando Hernández said on 12 October 2018 that personally as a Christian he is against same-sex marriage, and the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association urged President Xiomara Castro to stop 'immoral laws'. At the same time, trans visibility has grown: a trans activist and Asociacion Cozumel Trans co-founder ran for Congress in Francisco Morazan for the PINU party at the 26 November 2017 election, potentially the first openly trans officeholder, receiving 11,112 votes and placing 136th for a 128-seat National Congress; Kendra Stefani Jordany won a 2017 primary, Claudia Spellman ran for LIBRE in 2012, and Victoria Gomez sought asylum in Spain after threats and attacks in Tegucigalpa. About 400 people marched in a pride parade in July 2017 in San Pedro Sula.

Protection machinery has a contested history. Initial efforts to register an LGBTQ rights group in the 1980s met government opposition or extended delays; the first organisations arose often in response to the HIV/AIDS pandemic, held no legal standing, and were essentially ignored by the Government apart from police harassment. In 2004 the Government extended formal recognition to three LGBTQ rights interest groups despite organised protests from the Catholic Church, Pentecostals and conservative legislators. International human rights organisations state that the military Government targeted LGBTQ people for harassment, abuse and murder.

Following the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 on access to marriage, Honduran activists filed suit with the Supreme Court in May 2018 to legalise same-sex marriage, while a second case was dismissed in November 2018 for technical errors. A bill for same-sex marriage was presented to the National Congress in May 2022 by Libertad y Refundacion deputy Manuel Rodriguez and remained under discussion as of 24 May 2022.

The only general social-conditions statement available is that there is a social environment of historical discrimination against LGBTQ persons motivated by prejudice and machismo; the sources document no statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.
tangentialFactors:
Honduras and El Salvador are identified by the LAWG Education Fund as among the world's highest rates of violence against women and LGBTI persons, placing Honduras in a regional pattern rather than an isolated national one. A Reuters feature on Central America's LGBT people being terrorised at home and fleeing for their lives was returned HTTP 401 and could not be retrieved at research time, so its specific claims are unavailable.

The GlobalGayz Honduras archive provides a dated index of LGBT news from 2004 to 2011 with embedded excerpts, recording an August 2004 church protest at state recognition of three gay groups, 2009-10 items on an LGBT activist murdered amid violence and impunity, extreme violence against the gay community and post-coup abuses, and 2005 coverage of marriage and adoption bans. These dated items corroborate the violence timeline for Honduras.

Raw counts of LGBTQ killings reported for Honduras (174 violent deaths 2009-2014; 264 murders 2009-2017) are given by the source without population denominators and are not per-capita rates; they should not be read as a comparative risk ranking against other jurisdictions.
